pathway.title: Karman Holdings Inc. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: Net leverage has risen with each acquisition. The issuer's total debt principal was USD 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 against USD 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025, almost all of it the term loan upsized to fund the Seemann acquisition, so net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and, with finance lease liabilities that sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA, from 3.81x to 4.57x. Because LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from closing, the ratio probably overstates pro forma leverage, but the sources do not allow that to be measured. On unadjusted EBITDA the same net ratio is 4.54x, so the add-backs of USD 21,150 thousand (11.8% of LTM Adjusted EBITDA) matter to how leveraged the issuer looks. [Analyst Interpretation, based on CP-1 leverage and the CP-1A acquisition timeline.]

The issuer does not yet generate free cash. Operating cash flow was USD (22,119) thousand in FY2025 and USD (2,975) thousand in the six months to June 30, 2026, and operating cash flow less capex was USD (27,671) thousand on an LTM basis, as contract assets rose from USD 156,298 thousand to USD 187,120 thousand. Interest, capex and acquisitions were therefore paid from new debt and, in 2025, the IPO. The mechanism is revenue recognized over time ahead of billing, so growth consumes cash until contracts bill and collect. [Documentary Fact for the figures; Analyst Interpretation for the mechanism.]

Liquidity and maturities are the main support. Cash of USD 51.741 million plus an undrawn revolver of USD 150.0 million gave USD 201.741 million at June 30, 2026, scheduled amortization is about USD 5.050 million a year with USD 481.517 million shown as due thereafter in the December 31, 2025 schedule, the term loan matures on April 1, 2032 and the revolver on April 1, 2030. The one financial covenant is springing at 6.50x on a first lien net leverage basis and applies only when the revolver is drawn beyond a threshold the sources do not state, so lenders have no maintenance test while it is undrawn. [Documentary Fact.]

Customer and counterparty concentration is the main business risk. The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and no single program exceeded 12%, so revenue depends on a few primes even though the program base is broad. The filer's claim of sole or single source positions is management language and is not independently verified. [Documentary Fact for the percentages; Management Language for the positions.]

Reported information is less reliable than a clean filer's. Material weaknesses in internal control were reported as not remediated at June 30, 2026, Seemann purchase accounting was revised in the second quarter and judged immaterial, and the filings conflict on the Seemann consideration (cash of USD 210.0 million in the annual report against approximately USD 215.9 million cash and USD 232.9 million total consideration later), the term loan size (USD 767.8 million against USD 772 million) and end-market revenue shares. Each is logged and not reconciled. [Documentary Fact.]

runs.text: Demand and positioning. The issuer supplies payload protection, interstage and propulsion systems to US missile, hypersonic, launch and maritime programs, and management says it often holds sole or single source positions. The mechanism is that qualified suppliers are rarely requalified, which supports revenue durability, but the claim is management's. [Management Language, CP-1A company and operating model rows.]

Earnings scale and margin. LTM revenue was USD 589,552 thousand and LTM Adjusted EBITDA USD 179,068 thousand, a margin of 30.4%, with gross margin of 41.7% LTM against 38.3% in FY2024. Higher earnings are what reduces leverage if debt stays flat. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]

Liquidity and maturity profile. Liquidity of USD 201.741 million at June 30, 2026, an undrawn revolver of USD 150.0 million, and a current portion of notes of USD 5.610 million with the term loan due April 1, 2032 mean no refinancing event is near. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]
Program breadth. No single program was more than 12% of revenue, which limits single-program loss risk even with customer concentration. [Documentary Fact, CP-1A.]

Interest burden covered. LTM Adjusted EBITDA covered cash interest paid 3.37x, 3.24x in FY2025, and the August 3, 2026 repricing lowers future cash interest. [Documentary Fact for the ratios; Analyst Interpretation for the direction of future interest.]

Leverage drift. Net debt over Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and total debt over Adjusted EBITDA from 3.49x to 4.29x, because debt grew faster than LTM earnings. The mechanism is debt-funded acquisitions whose earnings enter LTM only from closing. [Documentary Fact for the ratios; Analyst Interpretation for the cause.]

Cash conversion. Negative operating cash flow and negative free cash flow after capex, with working capital absorbing cash as contract assets grow. Cover falls to 2.74x after deducting LTM capex, and 2.97x on unadjusted EBITDA. [Documentary Fact, CP-1.]

Concentration. The three largest customers were approximately 51.5% of FY2025 revenue and one supplier was 23.8% of accounts payable at December 31, 2025. A resourcing, funding or payment change at one prime would hit revenue and receivables together. [Documentary Fact, CP-1A.]

Acquisition dependence and add-backs. Four acquisitions closed between April 2025 and February 2026 and a fifth is pending; transaction, integration and lender fees recur as add-backs of USD 21,150 thousand LTM. The mechanism is that EBITDA quality depends on a recurring set of items. [Documentary Fact; Analyst Interpretation.]

Reporting reliability and thin lender protection in the sources. Unremediated material weaknesses, revised purchase accounting, five conflicts, an undisclosed owner base and no supplied credit agreement mean lender protections, guarantors and security cannot be confirmed. Missing evidence here is not an adverse conclusion; it limits confidence. [Insufficient Information for ownership and covenant terms.]

Floating-rate exposure. The term loan is priced at SOFR plus 2.25% from August 3, 2026, and no interest rate hedge was found in the sources searched, so cash interest moves with rates. [Documentary Fact; absence of hedges is Insufficient Information.]

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: This section is prose only. The facts are ordered by date and each states its status at the cutoff.

Financing history. Before April 2025 the company borrowed under a TCW financing agreement, which was extinguished when the company entered the Citibank credit agreement on April 1, 2025 with a new $300.0 million term loan and a $50.0 million revolver, maturing April 1, 2032 and April 1, 2030 respectively (10-K FY2025 page:140). That agreement has been amended five times to the cutoff. The First Amendment on May 27, 2025 added $75.0 million of term loan to fund the ISP acquisition; the Second Amendment on October 24, 2025 added $130.0 million to fund Five Axis and repay revolver borrowings (10-K FY2025 page:140). The Third Amendment on February 2, 2026 refinanced $502.8 million of existing term loans to a margin 75 basis points lower and added $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fourth Amendment on March 9, 2026 raised revolver commitments by $100.0 million to $150.0 million and removed the cap on incremental revolving commitments (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fifth Amendment on August 3, 2026 lowered the term loan margin to SOFR plus 2.25% and revolver pricing by 50 basis points (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19). All five are completed. Each of the three term loan increases coincided with an acquisition (ISP, Five Axis, Seemann), and MTI was funded by a $30.0 million revolver draw (10-K FY2025 page:141). That is the transmission mechanism: acquisition funding is arranged by amending the existing facility, whose springing covenant is written on a first lien ratio, and not by a new issue to bond investors, so no new notes were issued in the period. No bond, note issue or ratings event appears in the sources, and the run context lists no ratings.

Equity events. The IPO was completed on February 14, 2025: 26.5 million shares at $22.00, of which 8.4 million were sold by the company (10-K FY2025 page:116). On July 23, 2025 existing stockholders priced a secondary sale of 21,000,000 shares at $49.00, with an option for 3,150,000 more that was fully exercised, and the company "did not sell any shares or receive proceeds" (10-K FY2025 page:107). The company expects to retain earnings and has no current plans to pay dividends (10-K FY2025 page:87).

Acquisitions. MTI closed April 2, 2025 for $82.3 million in cash; ISP closed May 28, 2025 for approximately $52.9 million in cash and 147,842 shares; Five Axis closed October 28, 2025 for $90.7 million in cash and 68,625 shares (all 10-K FY2025 page:94). Seemann Composites and Materials Sciences, a maritime defense composites business, closed February 3, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15). The Q2 2026 10-Q states cash of approximately $215.9 million, shares valued at $17.0 million and total consideration transferred of $232.9 million, funded with incremental term borrowing, while the 10-K described the signed agreement as $210.0 million in cash and $10.0 million in shares (10-K FY2025 page:152); this is logged as a conflict and not reconciled. Seemann revenue was $37.8 million for the three months and $63.0 million for the six months ended June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16). Walker Precision Engineering, a Glasgow-based maker of components for missile seekers and guidance systems, is the subject of a definitive agreement dated July 20, 2026 for aggregate consideration of approximately $94.0 million, expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 subject to regulatory approvals (10-Q Q2 2026 page:29). Its status at the cutoff is pending as far as the sources show; funding, its earnings and any financing are Not supplied. It would be the first non-US operation described in the sources read, since the listed subsidiaries are in US states (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4); analyst interpretation: that adds cross-border integration and export-control questions the filings do not address.

Effect on leverage and liquidity. Per the financials handoff, total debt principal rose to 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 from 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025 and net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA reached 4.00x. The debt increase is the Seemann funding. Cash and the undrawn revolver gave 201.741 US$m of liquidity, and the handoff's illustration shows the pending Walker consideration would consume 46.6% of it if funded entirely from liquidity; the sources do not say how it will be funded. The expected annual interest saving from the repricing is described by management as "approximately $4 million" (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). Seller notes and contingent consideration: the 2024 seller note was repaid in April 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:141), and the Seemann acquisition has no contingent consideration (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15).

The increase has a mechanical cause that the sources show: the Third Amendment of the credit agreement raised the term loan by $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18) to fund the Seemann acquisition completed February 3, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:15), while LTM EBITDA carries Seemann only from that date and the filer states that pro forma information was impracticable (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16), so the ratio is probably overstated relative to a pro forma figure that the sources do not allow us to compute. Operating cash flow was negative for FY2025 and for the six months to June 30, 2026, because contract assets and receivables grew with revenue; with capital expenditure included, free cash flow was negative in every period shown except FY2024. Interest cover is moderate (3.37x LTM on Adjusted EBITDA versus cash interest paid) and falls to 2.74x after deducting LTM capex. Liquidity is adequate: cash and an undrawn $150.0 million revolver. The debt has no maturity before the term loan's April 1, 2032 date other than scheduled amortization of 5.050 US$m a year in the December 31, 2025 table and a current portion of 5.610 US$m at June 30, 2026, but the credit agreement itself is not supplied, the term loan size is stated two ways, and the filer reports material weaknesses in internal control. fields.value: View: Karman is a supplier of mission-critical structures, interstage systems and propulsion components to prime contractors on US missile, hypersonic, space-launch and, since February 2026, maritime defense programs. The credit story is demand-led growth that management is funding largely with acquisitions and term debt. Revenue visibility is high on paper, because the company says it often holds sole or single source positions on long-lived programs (10-K FY2025 page:17) and reports a large backlog (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). Three features limit how far that visibility supports debt service. First, concentration: the three largest customers were about half of FY2025 revenue (10-K FY2025 page:25), so a single prime's resourcing or funding decision moves the group. Second, the backlog definition was widened in 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33) and remaining performance obligations are a narrower measure (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7), so backlog growth cannot be read as the same kind of coverage as in the annual report. Third, the growth rate depends on acquired businesses: Seemann contributed revenue from its acquisition on February 3, 2026 (amounts in the transaction section), and the filer states that pro forma information is impracticable to obtain (10-Q Q2 2026 page:16). The ownership position is not documented in the pack: the 10-K incorporates ownership, related-party and director information by reference to a proxy statement that is not supplied (10-K FY2025 page:156), the run context names no sponsor, and a July 2025 secondary offering shows existing stockholders selling (10-K FY2025 page:107). Governance evidence is mixed: documented actions show equity raised at IPO, no dividends and no debt-funded distributions in the periods covered, but also five credit agreement amendments in the sixteen months from April 1, 2025 to August 3, 2026, and disclosed material weaknesses in internal control (10-K FY2025 page:153; 10-Q Q2 2026 page:41). Leverage and liquidity consequences are those in the financials handoff; this module adds the business mechanics behind them.

fields.value: Financing history. Before April 2025 the company borrowed under a TCW financing agreement, which was extinguished when the company entered the Citibank credit agreement on April 1, 2025 with a new $300.0 million term loan and a $50.0 million revolver, maturing April 1, 2032 and April 1, 2030 respectively (10-K FY2025 page:140). That agreement has been amended five times to the cutoff. The First Amendment on May 27, 2025 added $75.0 million of term loan to fund the ISP acquisition; the Second Amendment on October 24, 2025 added $130.0 million to fund Five Axis and repay revolver borrowings (10-K FY2025 page:140). The Third Amendment on February 2, 2026 refinanced $502.8 million of existing term loans to a margin 75 basis points lower and added $265.0 million (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fourth Amendment on March 9, 2026 raised revolver commitments by $100.0 million to $150.0 million and removed the cap on incremental revolving commitments (10-Q Q2 2026 page:18). The Fifth Amendment on August 3, 2026 lowered the term loan margin to SOFR plus 2.25% and revolver pricing by 50 basis points (10-Q Q2 2026 page:19). All five are completed. Each of the three term loan increases coincided with an acquisition (ISP, Five Axis, Seemann), and MTI was funded by a $30.0 million revolver draw (10-K FY2025 page:141). That is the transmission mechanism: acquisition funding is arranged by amending the existing facility, whose springing covenant is written on a first lien ratio, and not by a new issue to bond investors, so no new notes were issued in the period. No bond, note issue or ratings event appears in the sources, and the run context lists no ratings.

Walker Precision Engineering, a Glasgow-based maker of components for missile seekers and guidance systems, is the subject of a definitive agreement dated July 20, 2026 for aggregate consideration of approximately $94.0 million, expected to close in the third quarter of 2026 subject to regulatory approvals (10-Q Q2 2026 page:29). It would be the first non-US operation described in the sources read, since the listed subsidiaries are in US states (10-Q Q2 2026 page:4); analyst interpretation: that adds cross-border integration and export-control questions the filings do not address.

fields.value: Karman is a leveraged but liquid defense and space supplier whose credit profile is weakening as acquisition debt outpaces cash generation. What decides the outcome is whether acquired earnings and working-capital releases reduce leverage before the pending Walker acquisition, priced at about USD 94.0 million and not yet shown to be funded, draws on liquidity or adds debt.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Net leverage has risen with each acquisition. The issuer's total debt principal was USD 768,478 thousand at June 30, 2026 against USD 506,767 thousand at December 31, 2025, almost all of it the term loan upsized to fund the Seemann acquisition, so net debt over LTM Adjusted EBITDA rose from 3.25x to 4.00x and, with finance lease liabilities that sit outside notes payable and whose costs fall below EBITDA, from 3.81x to 4.57x. Because LTM earnings include acquired businesses only from closing, the ratio probably overstates pro forma leverage, but the sources do not allow that to be measured. fields.value: 7. New for the backlog review. Backlog per the annual report key-measure table 801,056 thousand at December 31, 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:99) and 1,322,124 thousand at June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33): growth 1,322,124 / 801,056 - 1 = 65.0%, equal to the company's 65%. Remaining performance obligations 550.6 million at December 31, 2025 (10-K FY2025 page:120) and 703.9 million at June 30, 2026 (10-Q Q2 2026 page:7): growth 703.9 / 550.6 - 1 = 27.8%. Backlog exceeds remaining performance obligations by 801.056 - 550.6 = 250.456 million at December 31, 2025 and by 1,322.124 - 703.9 = 618.224 million at June 30, 2026. Remaining performance obligations were 723.3 million at March 31, 2026 (10-Q Q1 2026 page:7), so they fell by 723.3 - 703.9 = 19.4 million in the second quarter while quarterly bookings were reported as nearly 500 million (EX-99.1 Aug 2026 page:1). The sources do not explain the divergence; it may reflect contract types in backlog that are not remaining performance obligations, which is an interpretation and not a finding.

fields.value: Corrected backlog statement for downstream use: the annual report carries two descriptions of backlog. The risk-factor paragraph says "contracts for which funding is appropriated or otherwise authorized" (10-K FY2025 page:35). The key-measure note says contract types "include but are not limited to purchase orders, long term agreements and contractual authorization to proceed" and "Backlog was previously referred to as funded backlog. No change to the historical dollar amount presented to the table above." (10-K FY2025 page:99). The 2026 quarterly report repeats the key-measure wording (10-Q Q2 2026 page:33). Whether the measure itself changed is therefore not established, and the handoffs' statement that the definition widened between the annual report and 2026 is withdrawn.
